items.title: Road Closures Follow Fatal Hit-and-Run Involving Pickup Truck in Mississauga
items.summary: According to CBC Toronto and Insauga, a pedestrian died Tuesday evening after being hit by a pickup truck in a hit and run at Winston Churchill Boulevard and Dundas Street West in Mississauga. Peel Regional Police say the victim, an adult, was struck by the vehicle and pronounced dead at the scene, though officers have not released further details about who was killed. A spokesperson with Peel Regional Paramedic Services confirmed only that the victim was an adult. Police shut down all eastbound and westbound lanes on Dundas Street between Hampshire Gate and Woodchester Drive through the Winston Churchill intersection while investigators worked the scene. Drivers in the area faced significant delays, and police urged motorists to avoid the intersection while emergency crews remained on site. Peel Regional Police are asking anyone with information about the crash to call their non-emergency line at 905-453-3311.

items.title: Council Approves Advisory Body to Track AI Data Centre Study and Report Back to Mississauga Residents
items.summary: According to Insauga, Mississauga city council voted Tuesday to create a Hyperscale Data Centre Task Force made up of councillors, city planning staff, industry stakeholders and members of the public. The temporary body is meant to keep residents informed as senior staff carry out a comprehensive review of large data centres and any new provincial rules that could regulate the fast growing industry. Ward 10 Councillor Sue McFadden brought forward the motion creating the task force, which is expected to provide regular updates and what the city calls transparent reporting for the public's benefit. The move comes two weeks after council unanimously approved an interim control bylaw imposing a one to two year moratorium on new large data centre developments in Mississauga. City officials say pausing new projects will give staff more time to study the issue and any regulations the province introduces before more facilities are approved.

items.title: City Warns Candidates of Daily Fees and Enforcement as Election Signs Appear Across Mississauga
items.summary: According to the City of Mississauga, election signs are starting to appear around the city ahead of the Oct. 26 municipal election, prompting officials to remind residents and candidates of the rules that govern them. The signs are allowed under the city's Sign By-law and do not require a permit, but campaigns that violate the rules face a $20 per day, per sign fee to cover storage costs if the City has to remove an illegal sign. City crews are proactively patrolling neighbourhoods and taking down signs placed illegally, and residents can report a suspected violation through the city's online service form or by calling 311. Officials ask residents not to move or remove election signs themselves on public property, though property owners can remove signs placed on their own land without permission. Every reported sign is reviewed by city staff, and those that break the by-law can be removed, with further enforcement action possible under the Provincial Offences Act. The city says the rules exist to keep roads, sidewalks and public spaces safe and to prevent visibility hazards for drivers and pedestrians.

items.title: Coroner Sets October Start Date for Inquest Into Fatal Police Taser Encounter in Malton
items.summary: According to Insauga, the province has scheduled a coroner's inquest into the 2019 death of Matthew DiGiovanni, a 34 year old Mississauga man who died after being shot with a Taser by Peel Regional Police at his family's home in the Malton area. Dr. Richard Wells, regional supervising coroner for the Central Region Toronto West Office, announced the inquest will begin in three weeks and run for about 10 days, hearing from roughly 12 witnesses over video conference. Dr. John Carlisle will preside over the proceedings, with Peter Napier serving as inquest counsel, the province's Ministry of the Solicitor General said in a news release. DiGiovanni died on Sept. 10, 2019 shortly after the encounter with police, and the inquest into his death is mandatory under Ontario's Coroners Act. The jury may make recommendations aimed at preventing further deaths, according to the province's release. The province describes an inquest as a public hearing conducted by a coroner, lawyer or retired judge before a jury of five community members.

items.title: Retail Stays Open While City Services Close for Truth and Reconciliation Day in Mississauga
items.summary: According to mississauga.com, most retail stores in Mississauga will stay open on Sept. 30 since the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation is not a statutory holiday in Ontario, even though most City of Mississauga services will be closed that day. The observance traces back to Sept. 30, 2013, when Orange Shirt Day, also known as Every Child Matters, began as a grassroots movement in Williams Lake, B.C. to honour residential school survivors, their families and those who never came home. The National Day for Truth and Reconciliation grew out of Call to Action 80 from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which asked the federal government to work with Indigenous communities on a day recognizing survivors and keeping the history of residential schools in public memory. Since June 3, 2021, the day has been marked as a federal statutory holiday, though the province of Ontario has not adopted it as one. The Art Gallery of Mississauga is among the local sites confirmed to remain open on Sept. 30, while hours for other city services vary by location.

items.title: Council Directs Staff to Study Bigger Fines as Illegal Dumping Complaints Keep Climbing in Mississauga
items.summary: According to Insauga, Mississauga city council has directed staff to explore tougher enforcement, including possible fine increases, to address a persistent illegal dumping problem. Current penalties for dumping household garbage and other items in parks, creeks and elsewhere already range from $500 to $100,000 for residents and businesses, though no specific new penalty amounts have been proposed yet. Staff were told at a Tuesday council meeting to study various options and report back at a later date, following a motion from Ward 5 Councillor Natalie Hart that also directs staff to identify recurring illegal dumping hot spots across the city. City officials said the municipality had already logged 195 dumping complaints in 2026 as of when they raised the issue in June, following more than 580 reports in 2025 and well over 2,000 complaints in total over the past few years. Items commonly dumped include car tires, paint cans, used furniture, construction waste, yard waste, propane tanks and household garbage.

items.title: Trade War Response Takes Center Stage as Four Contenders for Mississauga Mayor Debate at Board of Trade
items.summary: According to mississauga.com, four candidates running for Mississauga mayor met on Sept. 25 for a debate hosted by the Mississauga Board of Trade and co-hosted by CBC News at Sheridan College's Hazel McCallion campus. CBC's Nav Nanwa moderated the event, which brought together incumbent Carolyn Parrish, former mayor Bonnie Crombie, Ward 7 Councillor Dipika Damerla and Ward 2 Councillor Alvin Tedjo. Trade tariffs, transit and the future of Ridgeway Plaza were among the topics on the agenda. Asked how they would shield local businesses from the ongoing trade war with the United States, Crombie pointed to her record as former mayor, saying she helped attract more than $9 billion in investment and create tens of thousands of jobs. She proposed interest free deferrals on property taxes, lower business taxes, a guarantee that city suppliers get paid within 15 days, and a push to promote buying local while continuing to court outside investment. Damerla cited a Canadian Federation of Independent Business report ranking Mississauga 23rd out of 24 Ontario cities for ease of doing business, and pledged to move the city to first place to help tariff hit companies. Her plan also includes creating new jobs, considering property tax deferrals and encouraging residents to buy local.

items.title: Affordability, Transit and Fourteen Names on the Ballot Frame Thursday's Mississauga Mayoral Debate
items.summary: According to CityNews Toronto, four of the leading candidates for Mississauga mayor were set to debate Thursday night, moderated by CityNews reporter Mark McAllister, with election day set for Oct. 26. Fourteen candidates are officially running for the office, though recent polling points to a contest mainly between incumbent Carolyn Parrish, former mayor Bonnie Crombie and Ward 2 Councillor Alvin Tedjo, with Ward 7 Councillor Dipika Damerla still in the mix and a sizable share of voters undecided. Transportation was expected to be a central theme, with Crombie touting a transit platform that proposes extending the TTC's Line 2 subway west through Sherway Gardens into Mississauga's city centre, arguing residents lose too much time stuck in traffic. She has also pushed for stronger commitments from Metrolinx and the province to finish the Hazel McCallion LRT. Damerla built much of her campaign around fiscal accountability, renewing calls this week for the city to create an independent auditor general position to scrutinize spending and investigate complaints. Tedjo has leaned into affordability, unveiling a platform that includes a two year freeze on the residential share of Mississauga's property taxes and a permanent tax freeze for qualifying seniors.

items.title: City Partners With TRCA to Host Clothing and Electronics Drop-Off Drive for Circular Economy Month
items.summary: According to the City of Mississauga, October marks Circular Economy Month, an annual push to get residents repairing, donating and reusing belongings instead of throwing them out. The city notes that Canadians discard nearly 500 million kilograms of clothing and textiles every year, along with large volumes of electronics, even though roughly two thirds of those devices still work. To mark the month, Mississauga is partnering with the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority's Partners in Project Green program to run a collection drive from Oct. 12 to 25, with drop-off bins for unwanted clothing, textiles and electronics set up at 13 city facilities. The city frames a circular economy as simply getting more use out of what people already own rather than replacing it. Beyond the collection drive, Mississauga Library is highlighting its makerspace programs, which teach skills residents can use to repair broken items, build gifts or create projects out of recycled materials. Officials note that a library card unlocks far more than books, pointing residents toward these hands on programs as one more way to take part.

items.title: Peel Police Release Description of Missing 40-Year-Old Last Walking Her Dog Near Forum Drive
items.summary: According to Peel Regional Police, officers are searching for a missing 40-year-old woman, identified only as Hanna, who was last seen walking her dog on Sunday afternoon near Forum Drive and Eglinton Avenue in Mississauga. Police describe her as five feet four inches tall with a fair complexion and a medium build, with blond, shoulder-length hair typically worn in a messy bun. She was last seen wearing a grey T-shirt, a black puffer vest, navy blue jogging pants and black shoes with white soles. Her dog, a small animal weighing about two kilograms with light brown fur, was with her and was last seen wearing a black collar and red leash. Anyone with information on her whereabouts is asked to contact Peel police at 905-453-2121, extension 1233.
